chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Al-Hasan ibn Salih, who said:

I asked Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) about a man who divorced his wife while he was absent in another city, and he had two men bear witness to her divorce. Then he returned to her before the expiration of the waiting period (iddah) but did not bear witness to the reversion. Then he arrived at her after the expiration of the waiting period, and she had married another man. So he sent her a message saying: 'I had returned to you before the expiration of the waiting period, and I did not bear witness.'

He (the narrator) said, 'So he (peace be upon him) said: There is no way for him to her, because he acknowledged the divorce and claimed the reversion without proof. Thus, there is no way for him to her. And for this reason, it is fitting for the one who divorces to bear witness, and for the one who reverts to bear witness to the reversion, just as he bore witness to the divorce. And if he had reached her before she married, he would have been a suitor among the suitors.'

key_terms.رَجْعَة: Reversion (taking back the wife during the waiting period)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a man divorces his wife while away and claims he reverted without witnesses?
ai.summary: In this ruling from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him), the necessity of witnessing both the initial divorce and the subsequent retraction (raj'a) is emphasized to prevent disputes in cases of absence. The Imam clarifies that without witnesses for the retraction, the husband's claim is invalid, leaving the wife free to marry another; if she has not yet remarried, he becomes merely a suitor rather than the rightful husband. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that legal acts in family law require clear evidentiary proof to maintain social and legal order.
